html:
The Iñupiat are the Inuit of northern and northwest Alaska, from Norton Sound on the Bering Sea round to the Canadian border. They speak Iñupiaq.

Their ancestors were the Thule people, who spread east from Alaska across the Arctic around 1000 to 1200 and became the Inuit of Canada and Greenland. The Iñupiat stayed. On the coast they hunted bowhead whales from skin boats in spring, along with seals and walrus; inland groups followed caribou herds. Trade fairs linked them with Siberia and with Koyukon and other Athabaskan peoples to the south.

American whaling ships arrived in the 1850s and nearly wiped out the whales and walrus, and epidemics followed. Oil found at Prudhoe Bay in 1968 changed their land again: the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 created regional Native corporations, and the Iñupiat Arctic Slope corporation grew rich from oil. Whaling remains central to their culture. Their neighbours to the south are the Yup'ik.
sum: The Iñupiat are the Inuit of northern and northwest Alaska, from Norton Sound on the Bering Sea round to the Canadian border. They speak Iñupiaq.
